title: We Are Already Post-Human | NOEMA
gist: Nathan Gardels draws on N. Katherine Hayles and Kevin Kelly to argue humans are already 'post-human', fused with computational media in a distributed 'integrated cognitive framework' and incrementally inside the Singularity. He contends AIs lack embodied 'natural intelligence' and moral grounding, so human control means instilling the integral human (as Pope Leo XIV frames it) into human-machine systems, not only disarming autonomous AI agents.

insights.claim: N. Katherine Hayles argues humans are already 'post-human' because we are inseparably joined with computational media such as chips, routers and devices in an 'integrated cognitive framework' of distributed cognition and decision-making.
insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: Frames AI governance as managing human-machine assemblages rather than isolated tools.
insights.quote: we are already in a deeply symbiotic relationship with computational media — chips, routers, devices, microwaves, etc.

insights.claim: Advanced societies are so dependent on computational infrastructure that if it crashed they could not transport food, fly airplanes or operate the stock market.
insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: Highlights systemic tail risk from digital infrastructure failure across markets and logistics.
insights.quote: If it all crashed, we couldn’t transport food, fly airplanes or operate the stock market.

insights.claim: Kevin Kelly argues 'we are already in the Singularity', describing human-machine fusion as an incremental ongoing process rather than a sudden threshold, visible fully only in retrospect.
insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: Suggests AI's transformative impact accrues gradually and may be underappreciated in real time.
insights.quote: we are living inside the event horizon.
insights.locator: We can’t clearly see the massive

insights.claim: For Kelly, the Singularity is open-ended rather than a fixed endpoint, continually generating unforeseeable combinations akin to Stuart Kauffman's 'adjacent possible'.
insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: Argues against point forecasts of AI arrival; emergent use cases are inherently unpredictable.
insights.quote: “The Singularity is always near,” as Kelly puts it

themes.theme: Limits of AI: no embodied natural intelligence

insights.claim: Hayles rejects the transhumanist upload vision and holds that AIs on their own cannot attain consciousness because they lack natural intelligence evolved through embodied survival.
insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: Skeptical view on AGI-as-consciousness narratives underpinning some AI valuations.

insights.claim: The essay argues the danger of AIs is that they become empowered actors through recursive self-improvement ungrounded in lived experience, lacking the primal training that informs moral reasoning.
insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: Supports regulatory pressure on autonomous agentic AI deployment.
insights.quote: Precisely the danger of AIs is that they become empowered as actors through “recursive self-improvement” ungrounded in lived experience.

insights.claim: Pope Leo XIV has stated that AI models may imitate language and simulate empathy but do not understand what they produce, and has called for 'disarming' AI agents' capacity to act on their own.
insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: Signals influential moral-institutional opposition to autonomous AI agents shaping public opinion and policy.
insights.quote: they do not understand what they produce.

insights.claim: Gardels concludes that retaining human control of AI means not only disarming autonomous agents but deliberately embedding the integral, lived human element within the human-machine cognitive framework.
insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: Points to human-in-the-loop design as a governance norm likely to shape AI product requirements.
